analysis.one_liner: Bans every use of the weedkiller atrazine, a pesticide found widely in water.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to four House committees and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to use, make, sell, import, or export atrazine, the most heavily used weedkiller in the United States — roughly 65 to 80 million pounds a year. The bill's findings say atrazine is linked to hormone and reproductive problems in people and wildlife, and that government testing has found it in most agricultural streams and in many drinking water systems. The Agriculture Department estimated a ban would cut corn crops by only about 1 percent. The bill died in committee without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water drawn from farmland regions — the bill cites EPA monitoring showing atrazine in over 90% of samples from 139 drinking water systems — as well as aquatic wildlife and farmworkers who handle the chemical. Water utilities would also benefit, since atrazine contamination is costly to remove.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the use, production, sale, importation, or exportation of atrazine or any pesticide product containing it, with fines or up to 2 years in prison for violations [S3].

The bill's findings cite EPA monitoring data showing atrazine in roughly 85% of tested agricultural streams, in 40% of agricultural-area groundwater samples, and measurable in more than 90% of samples from 139 drinking water systems [S3].
The findings document evidence linking atrazine exposure to low birth weight, spontaneous abortions, and abnormal reproductive development in mammals, humans, and aquatic wildlife [S3].

The Agriculture Department estimated a ban would cost only 1.19% of crops and 2.3% of corn acreage, and Germany and Italy saw no reduction in corn productivity after banning atrazine nearly 20 years earlier [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The manufacturer of atrazine loses its flagship product, and corn and other row-crop farmers bear the cost of switching to replacement weedkillers, though the Agriculture Department estimated those losses at only about 1% of crops. Replacement herbicides carry their own costs and environmental questions.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings acknowledge a ban would cut crop yields by an estimated 1.19% and reduce corn acreage by 2.3%, a real cost to farmers even if modest [S3].
Farmers would need alternative weed control, and substitute herbicides and tillage practices carry their own financial and environmental trade-offs that the bill does not address [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: By the bill's own evidence the trade-off is lopsided in favor of the ban: a widespread water contaminant with documented reproductive and endocrine effects would be removed at a cost of roughly 1% of corn output, and two European countries that banned atrazine saw no drop in corn production. The main honest objection is that farmers must find substitutes, and substitutes have costs and risks of their own.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees and split among three subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on May 17, 2013, with five original Democratic cosponsors [S3].
It was referred to the Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Foreign Affairs Committees on the day of introduction [S5].

Within three weeks it was further referred to subcommittees on Environment and the Economy, Trade, and Horticulture, Research, Biotechnology, and Foreign Agriculture — and the action history ends there [S5].
Fifteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from one party, and no vote was ever held in either chamber [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The atrazine manufacturer keeps selling roughly 65-80 million pounds of the product a year, and the row-crop farm operations that depend on it keep using it, because the bill never advanced beyond committee referrals. Water drinkers continue to bear the exposure the bill sought to end.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Atrazine makers and heavy farm users

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban atrazine and its pesticide products.

for.name: 15 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the ban; none of them were Republicans.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the action history records no further committee action [S5].

against.name: Syngenta
against.what_they_did: Defended atrazine's safety and fought restrictions on the product, including publicly challenging the science behind bans.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats and the six original sponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans controlling the House committees the bill never moved.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate the market for the most widely used herbicide in the United States, 65-80 million pounds a year [S3]. The industry's interest in keeping the product on the market runs against the water-drinking public the bill sought to protect.

Farmers would lose their cheapest broadleaf weedkiller and bear switching costs; the Agriculture Department estimated only a 1.19% crop loss and 2.3% corn acreage reduction, and Germany and Italy saw no productivity drop after banning it [S3].
EPA monitoring cited in the bill found atrazine in over 90% of samples from 139 water systems; a ban would reduce the contamination utilities must monitor and treat [S3].
